newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-ENGLAND SEEK TO SILENCE TWICKENHAM SCORN.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-ENGLAND SEEK TO SILENCE TWICKENHAM SCORN.

text.p: England set out in search of a hat-trick of Five Nations championship titles on Saturday with captain Phil de Glanville appealing to the noisy Twickenham critics to unite behind the home team.

The visit of Scotland to a ground where they have failed to win for 14 years should be an ideal start for a developing English team, but memories of the supporters' jeers which greeted last month's 20-18 win over Argentina are fresh in many minds.

Coach Jack Rowell has since been accused by his predecessors of preaching tactical "mumbo-jumbo" to his players and even de Glanville is concerned the most inventive, cutting-edge rugby may come from the Scots.
The new captain, in charge of his first Five Nations match, watched the Pumas game from the stands yet refuses to commit England to the adventurous style which would swiftly silence the boo-boys.

"I think everyone was disappointed with the Argentina game. We played poorly for a long while," said de Glanville, well aware England have failed to score a Calcutta Cup try against their oldest rivals for four years.
"Everyone realises the Five Nations is different. It becomes more than just a game of rugby and, to that extent, a win is what people would like to see.
"I hope we give the crowd an opportunity to get behind us quickly. We need to make Twickenham a place that is uplifting for us and as hard work for the Scots as possible."

De Glanville insists his side will be positive and attempt to cast off the strait-jacket mentality of previous years, but conceded that 'expansive' was still not a buzz-word in the English rugby dictionary. The selectors have shown their hand by recalling the steadier Paul Grayson at fly-half in place of Mike Catt, and there continues to be no room for the smooth-running Jeremy Guscott.
A poor display from De Glanville will increase the noise from the Guscott lobby, but the captain is determined to prove he is worth his place on merit.
"You can't have a captain who doesn't have the respect of his players and that means putting you body on the line and doing the job as a centre. I'm a firm believer in my own ability."

England have just one new cap in open-side flanker Richard Hill whose new club colleague at Saracens, Francois Pienaar, reckons should be in the test side "for some time", yet Scottish captain Rob Wainwright believes his side are capable of pulling off a result.

They paid a heavy price for a lack of defensive concentration in the 34-19 defeat by Wales two weeks ago, but have now moved Gregor Townsend to fly-half where he can give the English defence a wider variety of problems.
"I think they have one of the best fly-halves in the world," admitted de Glanville. "He can dictate and change a game just like that. We're going to have to watch him very closely.
"There is no question of us underestimating them. We have done that before and fell flat on our face."

Each side contains only one survivor from that famous day in 1990 when Scotland deprived Will Carling's England of a grand slam at Murrayfield, and there are more similarities with the corresponding fixture four years ago.
Then, England also voted for a change at number 10 with Stuart Barnes given a chance at fly-half instead of Rob Andrew.

Barnes, who duly inspired one of the tries of the championship for Rory Underwood to set up an English win, remembers popping into a off-licence to buy a few bottles of wine the following day and being handed them for free by the appreciative shop-owner.
If Grayson can do something similar and kick his goals as well, England will be drinking to a record eighth successive victory over the tartan army.
